pr_title: Augment rand argument parsing to allow scaling
pr_body:
Extend opts parsing to parse long long values, and use it to have openssl rand accept requests for more than 2^32-1 bytes of data

Fixes #22622
pr_comments:
I guess you meant to write `openssl rand`, not `opt rand` (commit message & pr title)?

> allow `openssl rand` to accept larger data requests

A general remark:  just doing a `goto opthelp;` without printing any useful error message will create a lot of frustration for the app user, because he will only see the same usage message over and over again until he guesses what he messed up. (I know this from my own experience).
@nhorman Do let us know when you want a full review (this is still a draft PR)
@tom-cosgrove-arm ack, I think its ready now

I very much appreciate that you try to avoid force pushes, but now is a good time to do an interactive rebase in order to cleanup your history. If you do it without moving the merge-base (`git rebase -i --keep-base ...`) it will be easy for the reviewers to verify that you didn't introduce any tree changes, using GitHub's force-push diff.

Please note, that the commit message is outdated, the terabytes are still missing.

```
Augment rand argument parsing to allow scaling

Instead of just accepting a number of bytes, allows openssl rand to
accept a k|m|g suffix to scale to kbytes/mbytes/gbytes

Fixes #22622
```

I'd also appreciate if you'd change your PR title to match the subject line of the commit:  **Augment rand argument parsing to allow scaling**

And be warned: I will insist on strict parsing of the suffixes (with a meaningful error message). Or do you really want to get a bug report because someone called

```
openssl rand 10km
```

and didn't get 10 kilometres of random output? :wink:

At least in the commit message and the documentation (usage, manpage) we should use the correct official abbreviations [KiB](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kibibyte) / [MiB](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mebibyte) / [GiB](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibibyte) / [TiB](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tebibyte) for clarity:

    accept a [k|m|g|t] suffix to scale to KiB/MiB/GiB/TiB

_(BTW: I noticed that @jirka-h forgot to request support for [PiB](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pebibyte))_ 😉

**Fun Trivia**: NIST has a really neat page about [Prefixes for binary multiples](https://physics.nist.gov/cuu/Units/binary.html), which applies in particular to the section about the **historical context**.

> (BTW: I noticed that @jirka-h forgot to request support for PiB) 😉

:smile: Check `man head` - it supports prefixes all the way up to YiB (2^80). That's future ready:-)

Joking aside: SP 800-90C limits DRBG output to 2^64 bits per instantiation. We can go up to EiB (2^60). I have been testing RNGs (batteries of statistical tests) in the past (~6 years ago), going up to 128 TiB. With today's HW, reaching PiB is no problem -  `openssl rand` achieves rate of around 1.5GiB/s on my laptop, meaning you can generate 1PiB in just ~6 days on decent HW.

I think case insensitivity is a mistake here, we should use the correct official abbreviations both in the documentation **and** parser.  Althernatively, we should adopt the `dd(1)` convention as I [mentioned above](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/22624#discussion_r1385537852).

To add to the confusion, @mspncp asked for it [here](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/22624#discussion_r1383647049) and not [here](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/22624#issuecomment-1798285467).  We should be consistent.

Not an all that serious sugestion but it would be possible to uninstantiate and then reinstantiate the DRBG as we approached the 2⁶¹ byte limit.  The lifecycle transitions permits this:

![Rand lifecycle](https://www.openssl.org/docs/man3.1/man7/img/rand.png)

> I think case insensitivity is a mistake here, we should use the correct official abbreviations both in the documentation **and** parser. Althernatively, we should adopt the `dd(1)` convention as I [mentioned above](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/22624#discussion_r1385537852).
> 
> To add to the confusion, @mspncp asked for it [here](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/22624#discussion_r1383647049) and not [here](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/22624#issuecomment-1798285467). We should be consistent.

Ok, let's not start overengineering this. First of all, the intention was to only add binary multipliers and we should stick with that.

I would be ok with using all capitals (K,M,G,T), but not with all lowercase (k,m,g,t). The latter is what @nhorman initially used and the case-insensitivity was suggested by me only to avoid endless discussions about lowercase vs. uppercase.

With uppercase letters we would be consistent with `dd(1)`  https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/22624#discussion_r1385537852 and `head(1)` https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/22624#discussion_r1385600131.

> Ok, let's not start overengineering this.

Poor @nhorman probably already regrets having started to tackle this problem :wink:.
While we could reinstntiate, users can also just do $(openssl rand max ; openssl rand max) ad nauseum as a workaround.  I'd suggest we get the scaling committed and then tackle true unending output

> Not an all that serious sugestion but it would be possible to uninstantiate and then reinstantiate the DRBG as we approached the 2⁶¹ byte limit. The lifecycle transitions permits this:

Just for my education: why isn't automatic reseeding (which we do) considered sufficient? Why does FIPS mandate a complete reinstantiation?

> Just for my education: why isn't automatic reseeding (which we do) considered sufficient? Why does FIPS mandate a complete reinstantiation?

Absolutely no idea what the rationale behind this weird choice was.
Then let's add automatic reinstantiation and not bother the user with such nasty details.

IIRC the error recovery I implemented already does an automatic reinstantiation to recover from an error state. All we need to do is preventing the end-of-life error from being propagated to the user.

+1 to use {K,M,G,T} for binary prefixes (capital letters only), keep the support for `max` defaulting to 2^61 Bytes and close this issue. 

To exhaust 2^61 Bytes limit, ~45 years of runtime is needed assuming 1.5GiB/s rate. I think there is currently no need to implement the re-instantiate. This can be done later when we clarify/understand the rationale behind it. 

Thank you!
Jirka

Oh, midair collision. 

Just reading the last comments about the re-instantiation being in fact already implemented. When it's so, I agree to use it and replace `max` with `inf`. 

Thank you!
Jirka

IMO, the reinstantiation should be done at the EVP level not in the DRBGs -- fewer FIPS implications this way.  It might require a new param to indicate the maximum amount that can ever be produced in a single instantiation.  Still, not a concern in the near future.

> To exhaust 2^61 Bytes limit, ~45 years of runtime is needed assuming 1.5GiB/s rate.

Honestly, I see no reason then to reduce the maximum value of the `openssl rand` app from `SIZE_MAX` to `2^61`, nor would I even mention the theoretical limit in the manual page. When the first bug reports are raised in 45 years, it will not be our problem anymore.
And yes, @paulidale, I am aware that it will probably be sooner by Moore's law, but I will be retired by then 😁

> And yes, @paulidale, I am aware that it will probably be sooner by Moore's law, but I will be retired by then 😁

Hmm, frankly, I don't follow. I think setting the limit to 2^61 Bytes and referring to the SP 800-90C is much cleaner solution. The next generation of programmers will be aware of the limit and can deal with that. 

Also, using `SIZE_MAX` can have unwanted side effects. For example, the value can get bigger in the future. Why to violate the SP 800-90C recommendation when we are nowhere near the limit of 2^61 Bytes?
Fair point.
To be clear I proposed using capital letters in the documentation but we should accept them case insensitively.

> To be clear I proposed using capital letters in the documentation but we should accept them case insensitively.

I strongly disagree.  We should respect case sensitivity and only accept upper case (assuming `dd` compatibility).
added a unit test to check suffix scaling

Currently, with this PR openssl rand supports the suffixes [k|m|g|t] in a case-insensitive manner.  Conversely, dd supports the following suffixes (from the man page):
c - 1 byte
w - 2 bytes
b - 512 bytes
kB - 1000 bytes  
K|KiB - 1024 bytes
MB - 1000^2 bytes
xM|M|MiB - 1024^2 bytes
GB=1000^3 bytes
xG|G|GiB - 1024^3 bytes
<pattern repeats for T|P|E|Z|Y>

Interesting note: dd documents kB as being 1000 bytes, but MB being 1000^2 (note the change of leading caps).  Not sure if thats a doc error, or an implementation oddity.  Thats the only reference beyond c/w/b that uses a leading lower case suffix. 

It may be worth noting that dd seems to make up its own notation patterns (The single letter capital variants map to the standard metric values (1000^x) while the 3 letter variants (x<V> and <V>iB) map to the historic Computer Science variants (1024^x).  In contrast the NIST page reference previously maps two letter mixed case patterns (Ki/Mi/etc) to the metric computations, and two letter all uppercase patterns (KB/MB/GB) to the binary computations.

I'm assuming that we're just ignoring the c/w/b prefixes here, as they are somewhat non-sensical for our use case.

FWIW, dd implements their suffix parsing via xstrtoumax, which greatly simplifies that work effort.  If we wanted to match their parsing, we could do the same thing of course, but xstrtoumax wasn't introduced until [c99](https://en.cppreference.com/w/c/string/byte/strtoimax).  I'm not confident that all our supported platforms are going to have support for that call, which puts us in the position of, if we wanted to do this, effectively re-implementing significant portions of the xstrtol code from gnulib, or converting the switch statement we currently have to a significantly longer list of if (strcmp) {} else if (strcmp) statements.

Given that we document our prefixes and their case insensitivity, and that as I understand it the use case is most commonly to request, rather than an exact amount of data, more than is required, relying on the fact that a downstream consumer will terminate when enough data is read, I don't think we really need to worry about the metric annotations, allowing us to just do simple bit-shifting.  If we assume from above that, generally lower case isn't actually used in dd (i.e. that kB was realy meant to be KB in the docs page), I think it seems perfectly safe to just map the lower case values to their corresponding upper case binary power representation

Thanks for the detailed summary! 

> Interesting note: dd documents kB as being 1000 bytes, but MB being 1000^2 (note the change of leading caps). Not sure if thats a doc error, or an implementation oddity. Thats the only reference beyond c/w/b that uses a leading lower case suffix.

`coreutils` are using the same notation:
```
man tail
NUM may have a multiplier suffix: b 512, kB 1000, K 1024, MB 1000*1000, M 1024*1024, GB 1000*1000*1000, G 1024*1024*1024, and so on for T, P, E, Z, Y.  Binary prefixes can be used, too: KiB=K, MiB=M, and so on.
```
I think that current implementation (suffixes [k|m|g|t]) is sufficient.  We should definitively  update the **documentation** to use the capital letters. 

We can have a discussion if parsing should be case sensitive or not. I personally strongly vote to **make parsing case sensitive and follow the standard used by other tools.** 

My main argument is that if we allow lowercase prefixes people will start using them and surely enough, we will get complains that small letters should mean decimal prefixes. If we add support for decimal prefixes later to address the complains, it might break some existing scripts, causing headaches to end-users. 

So **let's do it right** from the beginning - let's allow CAPITAL prefixes only. Since `openssl rand` does not support any prefixes in the moment, there will be no confusion. Users will be forced to use capital prefixes which are clearly defined, not allowing any issues later. 

My 2 cents.

Thank you
Jirka

FWIW, I just tested dd, and that discrepancy does seem to be a dd scaling consistency error:
```
[nhorman@hmsvengance ~]$ dd bs=1 count=1kB if=/dev/urandom of=./test.bin
1000+0 records in
1000+0 records out
1000 bytes (1.0 kB) copied, 0.00578477 s, 173 kB/s
[nhorman@hmsvengance ~]$ dd bs=1 count=1KB if=/dev/urandom of=./test.bin
1000+0 records in
1000+0 records out
1000 bytes (1.0 kB) copied, 0.00653844 s, 153 kB/s
[nhorman@hmsvengance ~]$ dd bs=1 count=1K if=/dev/urandom of=./test.bin
1024+0 records in
1024+0 records out
1024 bytes (1.0 kB, 1.0 KiB) copied, 0.00675627 s, 152 kB/s

```
So:
kB produces 1000 bytes (which is consistent if we assume lowercase == decimal scaling)
KB produces 1000 bytes (which is inconsistent with the idea that uppercase produces binary scaling)
K produces 1024 bytes (which is consistent with the idea that uppercase produces binary scaling)

I'm ok with making the assumption that uppercase should be binary scaling, and only strictly accepting uppercase, as it leaves some wiggle room in the future, but I think we need to be clear here that there isn't a real 'right' to be had here. What we're doing isn't going to be completely in line with any of the coreutils, unless we want to make use of xstrtoumax, which comes with its own problems.


so

> Interesting note: dd documents kB as being 1000 bytes, but MB being 1000^2 (note the change of leading caps). Not sure if thats a doc error, or an implementation oddity. Thats the only reference beyond c/w/b that uses a leading lower case suffix.

This makes perfect sense (for those who aren't in the remaining three non-metric bastions): _k_ is the SI prefix for 1,000, _M_ is the SI prefix for 1,000,000, _G_ is the SI prefix for 1,000,000,000, etc.  I.e. these are prefixing the _byte_ unit.
That things are confounded by _K_, _M_, _G_ not being prefixes and getting different meanings is a little annoying.

Part of the reason I think we should enforce case sensitivity is that `m` is the SI prefix for 0.001 which is nonsensical here.  I also agree with @nhorman's point about retaining flexibility.


> I'm assuming that we're just ignoring the c/w/b prefixes here, as they are somewhat non-sensical for our use case.

Actually, I think _b_ (for block) might be useful for the use case described in #22622.  Hard disc sizes are displayed in blocks typically.  Agreed about _c_ and _w_ not being much use here.

But 512 is a legacy block size.  I'd hate to implement b, and have someone assume it mapped to whatever the block size of the device was, or to assume it was a more modern representation size (4096 or 8192). 

Either way it sounds like there is generally support for only accepting upper case prefixes (up to T for now).  Unless @mspncp strongly objects I'll make the change in the am

Not having _b_ is fine by me, it was a random brain fart.

@mspncp looks to be [okay with only upper](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/22624#issuecomment-1800182364).

Fair point, you are right.

To be honest, I only looked at the source code and didn't compile and test it. But it looks to me like the app loops over the suffixes and every suffix overwrites the previous one, such that `10KM` effectively becomes `10M`, right? A simple check for `shift != 0` before the switch statement with an error message about multiple suffixes would have prevented this.

issue_context.title: openssl rand - please allow to generate more than 2 GiB of data.
issue_context.body:
Hello,

could you please consider enhancing `openssl rand` to generate more than 2GiB of random data?

```
$openssl rand 2147483648
rand: Value "2147483648" outside integer range
rand: Use -help for summary.
```
The current limit of `2^31-1` Bytes seems to be arbitrary. For example, when preparing a hard-drive for the encryption, you need to fill the entire drive with random data first. Ideally, `openssl rand` should allow much higher limit, possibly 2^63-1 Bytes or even an endless stream of random data (for example when `openssl rand 0` is used). 

Thanks a lot!
Jirka
comments:
https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/22624

It seems easy enough to do, but I'm not sure its the right thing to do for a few reasons:
1) 2^63-1 isn't any more or less arbitrary a limit on request size than 2^32-1
2) parsing 64 bit values requires the use of strtoll, which, while part of POSIX 2008, might not be supported on all platforms that openssl supports
3) The easy workaround in either case (including the unending case), is something of the form:
$(while true; do openssl rand <value>; done)

Instead of just accepting larger integers on the command line, it would be more user friendly to introduce a new `size_t` valued command line argument type, which allows using the common size suffixes like `256k`, `30M`, or `8G`.
@mspncp I could get behind that approach.

Note: I wouldn't care about the suffixes for the [powers of 10](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gigabyte), only about the [powers of two](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibibyte) (i.e., `1G = 1GiB`, etc.). Those can be implemented easily by bit-shifting combined with an overflow check.

_(corrected: links where swapped)_

+1 to support binary suffixes. This how coreutils handles it as well - see for example `man head` or source code here:
https://github.com/coreutils/coreutils/blob/56e9acb2927874770363462cc6f5d2ee7d2b4c6d/src/head.c#L910

Thank you!

SP 800-90C limits DRBG output to 2⁶⁴ **bits** per instantiation.  That 2⁶¹ bytes.
There are reseed rules that kick in earlier but they are only reseedings & should be handled already.

Thank you!

Could we add support for TiB as well?
Surely there is a better way to do this than using openssl rand.  `dd if=/dev/urandom of=/dev/hdd bs=1M` perhaps?

There is a HUGE difference in performance (by factor 5x) between `/dev/urandom` and `openssl rand`


```
dd if=/dev/urandom bs=1M  | pv > /dev/null
312MiB/s

openssl rand 2000000000 | pv > /dev/null
1.56GiB/s
```

review_comments:
for platforms where sizeof(size_t) == 4, this case isn't required and will produce undefined behaviour according to _6.3.7 Bitwise shift operators_ in the C89 standard:

> If the value of the right operand is negative or is greater than or equal to the width in bits of the promoted left operand. the behavior is undefined.

I.e. we should detect this case and error.

Something along the lines of
```c
if (shift / 8 >= sizeof(size_t))
    …
```
before line 165 where the shift is first done.
I just noticed we don't have a left shift operation in safe_math.h. Could be nice to have in future.
Good suggestion.  Both directional shifts could be added.  I'm not sure there is an error condition though.  Shifting too far would produce 0 (for unsigned) and 0 or -1 for signed.
If we use uint64_t above, I think we avoid this problem entirely and lets us keep T, but I agree adding a safe left shift operation is a good idea.
